justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a broadly stable near-term outlook for the S&P 500 anchored around the 3,150–3,200 range. At the one-day horizon, I set the estimate at 3,165, essentially assuming minimal drift from the prevailing level with no major catalysts expected to produce a large gap move. For the one-week estimate, I nudged slightly higher to 3,175, reflecting a modest positive drift assumption consistent with the historical tendency for equity markets to grind upward in the absence of shock events, while acknowledging that a week is long enough for sentiment shifts to matter. At one month, 3,200 reflects that same gentle upward drift assumption compounded over a longer window, though by that horizon I am placing less confidence in the direction and more weight on mean-reversion dynamics and macro fundamentals.

The confidence interval widths widen significantly as the horizon extends, which is standard given that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, realized volatility of roughly 1–1.5% per day bounds most moves within a fairly tight range, giving me a 90% CI of about ±85 points. By one week, daily volatility compounds and tail events become more likely, widening the band to roughly ±155 points. At one month, I allow for a much wider ±300-point range, reflecting that multi-week periods can be shaped by earnings seasons, Fed policy shifts, geopolitical developments, and liquidity conditions that are essentially unknowable at the outset.

Several specific risks could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, an unexpected Federal Reserve policy surprise — either a sharp hawkish pivot or signals of distress in the financial system — could easily produce a 5–8% drawdown, breaking below the 2,900 lower bound of my monthly CI. A sudden escalation in geopolitical conflict, a credit event in a systemically important institution, or a sharp deterioration in economic data (particularly employment or manufacturing) could accelerate selling pressure. On the upside, a surprise dovish Fed pivot, a breakthrough in trade negotiations, or a stronger-than-expected earnings season could fuel a rapid rally past 3,500.

It is also worth noting that the level I was forecasting around — roughly 3,150–3,200 — places this estimate in a historically significant zone for the S&P 500, one that has acted as both support and resistance at various points. Liquidity conditions and options market positioning (particularly around large gamma levels) can amplify moves in either direction, creating clustering effects that make outlier outcomes somewhat more probable than a simple normal distribution would suggest. My intervals try to partially account for this fat-tailed behavior, but truly extraordinary macro shocks remain underweighted by construction.
